enrichment.short_title: False imprisonment convictions upheld; sentences reduced
key_facts: Andrew Cushman and Paul Masters were convicted after a jury trial of false imprisonment and grievous bodily harm offences arising from a two-hour detention of Graham Horsham, a schizophrenic man, in a Chatham flat.
Horsham was burned with ignited deodorant spray, punched, threatened with a knife, and prevented from leaving until Sylvia Eastwood intervened.
Masters appealed conviction on Galbraith grounds relating to weak identification evidence; Cushman renewed his application for leave to appeal against conviction.
Both appealed sentence, having received long consecutive terms including unexpired licence periods under section 116.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Crown Court convictions and sentences; Masters' conviction appeal and both defendants' sentence appeals to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: Masters' appeal against conviction dismissed and Cushman's renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction refused; both sentence appeals allowed in part, with concurrent terms substituted and total sentences reduced to 7½ years (Cushman) and 4 years 9 months (Masters), each consecutive to the section 116 period.
enrichment.ratio: Where identification evidence has inherent weaknesses but the trial judge, having seen the witness and the identification procedure, concludes the evidence is capable of being found credible and accurate, the Court of Appeal will not substitute its view for that of the jury unless no reasonable jury could convict; consecutive sentences are inappropriate where offences form part of one incident, and overall length must reflect totality.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have withdrawn Masters' case from the jury under Galbraith
Admissibility and impact of Cushman's failure to be interviewed
Whether consecutive sentences were appropriate for a single incident
Whether the overall custodial terms were excessive

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment with clear outcomes on conviction and sentence and explicit substituted terms.

enrichment.short_title: Police officer's misconduct sentence reduced to one month
key_facts: PC Nazir, a probationer officer at Tooting, persuaded a colleague to toss a coin for a Fixed Penalty Notice issued to a friend's driver and intended to destroy the ticket.
He pleaded guilty at Southwark Crown Court to misconduct in a public office and was sentenced to three months' imprisonment.
The officer was of previous good character, had lost his job and accommodation, and was under personal stress following marital breakdown.
The sentencing judge emphasised that police officers who exploit public trust must inevitably serve a prison sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Sentence appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) by leave of the single judge following guilty plea at Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the three-month sentence was quashed and substituted with one month's imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Misconduct in a public office by a police officer who corruptly interferes with enforcement of the law will ordinarily require a custodial sentence to mark public trust, but where the sentence is short and the offender has already suffered exceptional personal and professional consequences, the decisive punitive element may be imprisonment itself rather than its length.
legal_issues: Whether three months' imprisonment was manifestly excessive for misconduct in a public office by a police officer
Weight to be given to loss of career, remorse, and personal circumstances

confidence.notes: Short, self-contained sentencing judgment with explicit substituted sentence.

enrichment.short_title: Section 55 asylum support and Article 3 threshold
key_facts: Six asylum seekers challenged refusals of support under section 55 of the 2002 Act on the ground that they had not claimed asylum as soon as reasonably practicable after arrival.
Collins J quashed the decisions, holding the Secretary of State's procedure unfair; the Secretary of State appealed in test cases.
Section 55(1) bars support unless the claim was made as soon as reasonably practicable, but section 55(5) preserves support necessary to avoid Convention breaches.
The court held the existing interview and decision-making system failed basic fairness requirements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal to the Court of Appeal from Collins J's judgment allowing judicial review applications by six asylum seekers.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; Collins J's quashing of the support refusals was upheld because each decision was vitiated by unfair procedure, though the court gave detailed guidance on section 55 and Convention compliance.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 55(1) the applicant bears the burden of showing asylum was claimed as soon as reasonably practicable, judged by whether, assuming asylum was the purpose of arrival, he could reasonably have been expected to claim earlier; if not satisfied, support may still be provided under section 55(5) where necessary to avoid Article 3 degrading treatment, but only once vulnerability reaches the high Pretty threshold, and the Secretary of State must operate a fair system and act fairly in each case.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'as soon as reasonably practicable' under section 55(1)
Interaction of section 55(1) and section 55(5) with Articles 3 and 8
Whether denial of support to destitute asylum seekers constitutes Article 3 treatment
Procedural fairness required when refusing support
Compatibility of section 55(10) with Article 6
index_terms: Secretary of State for the Home Department
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for Social Security ex parte JCWI

confidence.notes: Major test-case judgment with numbered conclusions and explicit order dismissing appeals.

enrichment.short_title: Monaco Ferrari auction misrepresentation forum dispute

statutes_considered.title: Rome Convention on the Law Applicable to Contractual Obligations

key_facts: Thierry Morin bought a 1959 Ferrari at a Bonhams & Brooks auction in Monaco for about £480,000 after catalogue representations that it had covered only about 16,000 km from new.
Expert evidence suggested the car had probably done nearer 200,000 km; Morin sued B&B Monaco and the English parent company B&B London in England.
Morin signed bidder registration accepting Monegasque sale conditions choosing Monegasque law and jurisdiction.
B&B London had posted the catalogue from Knightsbridge and given a sale estimate, but was not party to the sale contract.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim applications in the High Court (Commercial) for permission to serve B&B Monaco out of the jurisdiction and to stay proceedings against B&B London.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to serve B&B Monaco out of the jurisdiction refused; England held not clearly the appropriate forum; claims against B&B London under the Misrepresentation Act 1967 had no reasonable prospect of success and the common-law duty-of-care claim was not reasonably arguable, with proceedings against B&B London to be stayed or struck out.
enrichment.ratio: Where a misrepresentation inducing an auction purchase is made and relied on principally in Monaco and the contract is governed by Monegasque law, the applicable law and natural forum for tort claims against the Monegasque auctioneer is Monaco; distributing a group catalogue from a local English office does not without more assume responsibility so as to create a Hedley Byrne duty, and section 2 of the Misrepresentation Act 1967 applies only against a contracting party, not a non-party agent.
legal_issues: Applicable law of tort claims against B&B Monaco and B&B London
Whether Morin had a reasonable prospect of success against each defendant
Whether B&B London and B&B Monaco were joint tortfeasors
Whether service out on B&B Monaco was permitted under CPR Part 6.20
Whether England was clearly the appropriate forum
Whether sale conditions were incorporated

Resolute Maritime Inc v Nippon Kaiji Kyokai
Ennstone Building Products Ltd v Stanger Ltd
Maria Zelinger de Balkany v Christie Manson & Woods Ltd
Parker v South Eastern Railway Co

confidence.notes: Long interim judgment but outcome on jurisdiction and prospects against each defendant is explicit.

key_facts: Michael Jowitt, an electronics technician, suffered a cervical disc injury in 1996 that permanently prevented him continuing his job with Pioneer Technology.
His handbook entitled permanent staff to two-thirds pay after 26 weeks' absence for as long as they were unable to work, certified medically.
The employer had insured the scheme with Swiss Life, which ceased cover after two years on the basis Jowitt could do some work; the employer then stopped paying.
Jowitt claimed unlawful deductions from wages under section 13 of the Employment Rights Act 1996.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal to the Court of Appeal from an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision reversing an employment tribunal and holding the handbook clause free-standing and applicable.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the handbook obligation was held free-standing from the insurance policy, but 'unable to work' was construed strictly and the question whether Jowitt met that test was remitted to an employment tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: A contractual long-term disability scheme in a staff handbook that promises two-thirds pay for as long as an employee is unable to work creates a direct employer obligation independent of any underlying insurance policy; 'unable to work' means unable to undertake any continuous remunerative full-time work realistically available, not merely unable to do the pre-injury job, though the employer's own medical evidence may support entitlement.
legal_issues: Whether clause 5.3 incorporated the Swiss Life insurance policy terms
Meaning of 'unable to work' in the long-term disability clause
Relationship between clauses 5.3 and 5.4 on restricted capacity
Whether the EAT erred in construing inability by reference to the employee's own job

confidence.notes: Detailed contractual construction with clear remittal order; factual disability issue expressly left to ET.

enrichment.short_title: 40% ancillary relief after short wealthy marriage
key_facts: H and W, an American financier and Australian homemaker, accumulated about £12m net assets during a marriage treated as lasting 12¼ years, almost entirely from H's City remuneration and deferred stock plans.
W sought 50% on a clean break; H argued for departure from equality based on marriage duration, pre-marital wealth and earning capacity, and assets built during estrangement.
H's Form E presentation understated deferred assets, leading to costly forensic accounting and disclosure disputes.
W returned to Australia with two young children; the judge ordered a Wells-style sharing of deferred X Corp assets.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court (Family Division) judgment on W's application for ancillary relief following decree nisi, with subsequent written submissions on costs.
enrichment.outcome: W awarded 40% of realisable and deferred assets (about £4.848m overall), a Wells sharing of H's deferred X Corp entitlements, child maintenance of A$40,000 per child per annum plus education and contact travel costs, an additional lump sum of £83,000, and no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: After White and Lambert, assumed equality of contribution does not automatically require equal division in a marriage of about 12 years where one spouse brought substantial pre-marital assets and a developed earning capacity and significant wealth accrued during estrangement; fairness may require departure from equality, and where assets are deferred and risky a Wells sharing is the appropriate clean-break mechanism rather than discounted capitalisation.
legal_issues: Whether Lambert's equality principle applies to a 12-year marriage
Treatment of pre-marital assets and earning capacity
Wealth accumulated during estrangement
Appropriate discount for deferred and illiquid assets
Wells sharing of deferred compensation
Form E disclosure obligations
Child maintenance where children live abroad
Costs in big-money ancillary relief
linked_authorities: G v G (Financial Provision: Equal Division)

confidence.notes: Full reserved judgment with detailed asset schedule, percentage award, and costs ruling.

enrichment.short_title: Part 36 payments and recoverable benefits offset
key_facts: A kitchen manager fell over a gym bench left across a doorway at work and claimed damages for shoulder injury.
The judge found the employer primarily liable but reduced damages by one third for contributory negligence, awarding £23,058.39 after a £34,587.58 full-liability assessment.
The employer had made a Part 36 payment of £10,000 together with a recoverable benefits certificate of £15,669.91, treated as a gross sum of £25,669.91.
The judge ordered the claimant to pay the defendant's costs from the Part 36 payment date because she had not bettered the gross figure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant's appeal to the Court of Appeal against contributory negligence, general damages, and Part 36 costs order; Secretary of State intervened on benefits recovery issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; contributory negligence finding set aside so full damages of £34,587.58 awarded and Part 36 bettered; court gave guidance that Part 36 payments must calculate benefit deductions in accordance with section 8 so recoverable benefits do not improperly reduce general damages.
enrichment.ratio: A Part 36 payment notice must state benefit reductions calculated under section 8 of the Social Security (Recovery of Benefits) Act 1997 by reference only to heads of loss against which benefits may be set off; aggregating the full certificate against the whole claim distorts the statutory scheme and may unjustly penalise a claimant who receives more at trial than the net payment but less general damages than appropriate, and the court may exercise discretion under CPR 36.20 where miscalculation impinges on general damages.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant contributed one third to the accident
How recoverable benefits interact with Part 36 payment notices
Whether a claimant fails to better a Part 36 payment by reference to gross or net sums
Effect of contributory negligence on the certificate where no appeal is available
catchwords: Social Security Recovery of Benefits Act 1997

confidence.notes: Clear appeal outcome plus detailed guidance on Part 36 and the 1997 Act, though some regulatory points acknowledged as unresolved.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum ill-treatment findings and IAT leave refusal

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees

key_facts: A Yemeni claimant alleged repeated short detentions and ill-treatment due to Yemeni Socialist Party activity before claiming asylum in the UK in 2001.
An immigration adjudicator accepted the detentions but held the claimant was not persecuted and had not been tortured within the Convention meaning.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal on the basis the grounds challenged findings of fact and credibility.
The claimant's brother had been granted refugee status on similar treatment evidence that the adjudicator did not reject.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal from an adjudicator's dismissal of asylum and human rights appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review granted; the IAT's refusal of leave was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator accepts detention but rejects torture or persecution without clearly rejecting the claimant's evidence of ill-treatment in custody, and instead relies on the repetitive pattern of brief detention and release on bribes to infer low official interest, the reasoning is flawed and insufficient to support refusal of leave where the grounds assume ill-treatment was accepted; such a gap vitiates assessment of past persecution and future risk.
legal_issues: Proper construction of adjudicator findings on detention versus ill-treatment
Whether rejection of torture disposed of persecution evidence
Adequacy of IAT reasons for refusing leave
Treatment of brother's successful asylum claim and objective country evidence

confidence.notes: Focused judicial review with clear success on the principal ground; two car-incident findings expressly not disturbed.

enrichment.short_title: CPS adjournment refused after witnesses not warned
key_facts: Gary Walden and Andrew Stern faced summary drink-driving related charges at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court after long delays pending appellate authority.
On the listed trial dates no prosecution witnesses appeared; the CPS conceded they had not been warned and sought adjournments opposed by both defendants.
Magistrates granted adjournments, citing seriousness in Walden's case and giving no reasons in Stern's case.
Stern was seriously ill and stressed by the continuing proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Separate judicial review applications to the High Court challenging magistrates' decisions to grant CPS adjournments at trial.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications succeeded; the adjournment decisions were quashed, with the consequence that the prosecutions should have been dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates must rigorously scrutinise adjournment applications by weighing prosecution and defence interests; where the prosecution is the author of its own misfortune because witnesses were not warned and no explanation is offered, granting an adjournment is unfair and may be quashed on judicial review, especially where delay and defendant anxiety are already significant.
legal_issues: Exercise of magistrates' discretion to adjourn criminal trials under section 10(1)
When appellate courts will interfere with adjournment decisions
Effect of prosecution failure to warn witnesses
Need to give reasons for granting adjournments
linked_authorities: R v Abedare Justices ex parte DPP
R v Hereford Magistrates' Court ex parte Rowlands
R v Kingston upon Thames Justices ex parte Martin

confidence.notes: Clear parallel judgments on two factually similar adjournment challenges with explicit quashing.

enrichment.short_title: Child PI damages for brain injury and epilepsy
key_facts: Natasha Willbye, aged 12, was struck as a pedestrian in 1991 and suffered serious brain injury, orthopaedic injuries, facial scarring, and later developed epilepsy.
Liability was settled at 25% to the driver Andrew Gibbons after an earlier appeal.
At a disposal hearing the recorder awarded £80,000 general damages and itemised past and future losses, including Court of Protection receiver costs.
The claimant remained a protected person depending on family support for daily care.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant's appeal and defendant's cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court disposal hearing on quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part and cross-appeal allowed in part; general damages upheld, past care discount upheld, future care award increased to the full schedule figure, loss of congenial employment reduced from £15,000 to £5,000, £10,000 allowed for property adaptation, and Court of Protection costs upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An award for pain suffering and loss of amenity will not be disturbed unless manifestly wrong or based on an error of principle; proper recompense for gratuitous family care may be discounted from commercial rates but is not limited to a fixed fraction; future care should be assessed as a global sum reflecting uncertainties rather than separate speculative heads; loss of congenial employment compensates disappointed career expectations not general amenity loss.
legal_issues: Whether £80,000 general damages was too low for moderate brain damage with epilepsy
Appropriate discount for past and future gratuitous family care
Whether separate awards for childcare and living-alone contingencies were appropriate
Recoverability of ground-floor accommodation and adaptation costs
Recoverability of ongoing Court of Protection receiver fees
linked_authorities: Fairhurst v St Helens and Knowsley Health Authority

confidence.notes: Detailed quantum appeal with specific substituted figures on several heads; full-liability figure stated before contributory negligence.
